item.title: What Everyone Should Understand About Fraysexuality
item.description:
Sexual Orientation

What Everyone Should Understand About Fraysexuality

Fraysexuality is a sexual orientation that challenges societal norms.

Posted June 8, 2026

Key points
  • Fraysexuality is part of the asexuality spectrum.
  • Fraysexuality describes strong sexual desire for people someone doesn't know well.
  • Fraysexuals tend to experience diminishing sexual desire once an emotional connection is established.
  • Fraysexuality is often misunderstood as an intimacy or attachment disorder, and unduly pathologised.
Source: VladOrlov / iStock

Do you have strong sexual desire for people you don’t know, but as soon as a romantic relationship is established, you lose your sexual desire for that person?

If you have noticed that this is your pattern, you might believe there is something wrong with you. You might have heard about “avoidant attachment style” and wondered if it was your problem.

Perhaps nothing is wrong with you. You could be a fraysexual.

Human sexuality is often discussed as a fixed linear and predictable trajectory: People meet, attraction grows, emotional intimacy deepens, and sexual desire strengthens. The dominant societal narrative tells us that the only “normal” is when two people are in a long-term monogamous relationship where sex keeps thriving, and that this is what we should aspire to. But human sexuality doesn’t always follow that narrative because there is much more diversity than that.

Fraysexuality is a sexual orientation that describes a person primarily experiencing sexual desire for people they don’t know well. As emotional intimacy increases, their sexual desire diminishes or disappears entirely. This orientation is often thought to be the opposite of demisexuality, in which sexual desire only emerges after emotional intimacy is established. Both fraysexuality and demisexuality are part of the wide spectrum of asexuality.

Fraysexuality is not discussed much, so many people are unaware of it. But when fraysexuals discover the there is a term for their orientation, it can validate their experience and be transformative because finally they no longer feel “broken”.

Fraysexuality is not a fear of commitment, getting bored in relationships—or a preference for casual sex. It is a pattern of sexual desire that forms a legitimate sexual orientation. People may identify with another sexual orientation too; some people are heterosexual and fraysexual, or gay and fraysexual.

A fraysexual person tends to feel intense sexual desire at the early stages of meeting someone. The excitement of novelty, mystery or unfamiliarity are some of the essential ingredients that make the sexual desire potent. However, once emotional closeness develops, sexual desire wanes although affection and romantic feelings for the person may remain intact. It is important not to conflate the absence of sexual desire with diminished love. In our society, the dominant narrative also tells us that emotional closeness and sexual desire are naturally connected, but it isn’t so for everyone. Fraysexual people do not follow this dominant script, and, as a result, they can feel shame, confused, self-doubting, and even feeling “broken”. It is also common for fraysexuals to be unduly pathologised as having an attachment disorder or an intimacy disorder in mental health settings if the clinician isn’t aware of fraysexuality.

Of course, it is common for sexual desire to diminish over time in any long-term relationship; that isn’t necessary a sign of fraysexuality. Some people do have attachment and intimacy issues and experience sexual or intimacy disconnection with their partners. Attachment and intimacy issues can always be explored in therapy, but not as a “cure” for fraysexuality.

As with other sexual orientations, fraysexuality exists on a spectrum and experiences vary widely between individuals. Some fraysexual people lose their sexual desire quickly, while others experience a gradual shift over time.

One common myth is that fraysexual people are incapable of love or commitment. In reality, many have stable long-term romantic relationship(s) with meaningful connections, but those connections may not involve sex. And while “sexless” relationships are perceived negatively in society, they may be well-fitted to fraysexual people. However, it is also common for fraysexual individuals and their romantic partner(s) to be in open relationships that allow them to live their lives authentically and in congruence with their orientation.

Within a relationship, honesty and clear communication skills are essential, as it can be tricky to explain fraysexuality to a partner. Often, people will perceive their partner’s waning sexual desire as a rejection. But in reality, a reduction in sexual desire does not automatically equate to a lack of depth, importance or meaning in a romantic relationship. What is important is for people to find a mutual understanding of how they want to conduct their relationships rather than forcing themselves to match societal expectations.

Labels are not helpful for everyone, but they can provide clarity and relief for people who have struggled to understand themselves and their sexuality. Discovering the label of fraysexuality can help individuals recognise that they are not alone and not “broken”. Such a label can help form a language in which more public discourse can happen, making fraysexuality more visible, and normalising it as being a part of natural human sexual diversity.

Human connection and sexual desire are more complex that the simple models society often promotes. Understanding that complexity can lead to a greater acceptance of human diversity, and lead us to be kinder towards each other’s differences.

item.title: Estrangement Doesn’t Happen All at Once
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Estrangement Doesn’t Happen All at Once

Distance in families usually develops over time.

Posted June 8, 2026

Key points
  • When an estrangement happens, those who are left behind often feel confused.
  • Estrangement can feel like a "bolt out of the blue," even when it's been in the works for some time.
  • Most of us assume that our close relationships are resilient enough to survive even big challenges.
  • Estrangement can happen between parents and children, siblings, and friends.

When we think about estrangement, whether it’s between parents and adult children, siblings, or close friends, we might imagine that there was a single moment when everything changed: a terrible argument, a final conversation, or a threat never to reach out again that is carried through.

The Myth of the "Defining Moment"

But for many people, estrangement doesn’t unfold that way at all. Instead, estrangement tends to develop gradually in ways that can be too easy to miss at first and too difficult to fully understand even in hindsight.

In close relationships, we expect our connections to be relatively resilient. After all, virtually every family or long-standing friendship will face and muddle through disagreements at some point in time. Also, in close relationships, emotions can run high, misunderstandings do happen, and often, things find their way back to equilibrium. Because of this expectation, early signs that something significant is shifting can be explained away.

Small Signs Can Be Easy to Miss

For instance, a text message might go unanswered. A call isn’t returned quite as quickly as it might have been in the past. Plans become harder to confirm. Conversations feel slightly different, even if nothing obvious has changed. When these things happen, few of us would immediately think, “This is the beginning of an estrangement.” Instead, we’re more likely to think, “They’re busy. Something else must be going on.”

And often, that is entirely true. But there are times when these small disruptions don’t resolve the way we expect them to. Instead, they accumulate.

Over time, people may begin to notice patterns that are harder to ignore. Certain topics now lead to tension more quickly. Attempts to talk things through don’t seem to bring the same sense of resolution they once did. What might have once been brushed off begins to feel more significant and is felt more deeply. It is less like a passing conflict and more like a shift in the relationship itself.

Efforts at Repair May Come Too Late

It’s often at this point that people begin trying, more intentionally, to repair what feels off. They reach out. They initiate conversations. They attempt to clarify misunderstandings or reestablish a sense of connection. These efforts can take many forms, but they tend to reflect the same underlying hope. People are hoping that whatever has changed can be addressed and restored.

Sometimes those efforts work, and sometimes, they don’t.

When attempts to repair the relationship don’t lead to the expected outcome, the experience becomes more confusing rather than less. People tend to find themselves rethinking earlier interactions and asking questions they didn’t think to ask before, like “Have things been like this for longer than I realized? Did I miss something? Is this something that can be fixed?”

It’s important to note that this process rarely unfolds in a straight line. There may be periods where things seem better, and the relationship feels back on an even keel. But then up pop moments where distance becomes more apparent again. There may be conversations that feel promising, even meaningful, without necessarily changing the overall direction of the relationship. This back-and-forth can make it especially difficult to recognize what is happening in real time, in the bigger picture.

A Turning Point Is Reached

At some point, however, there is a change. It is often subtle, but significant. A person begins to see the relationship differently than they did before. Questions about what is happening in the relationship may give way to questions about what is tolerable, sustainable, or possible moving forward.

For some people, this is the beginning of creating distance. For others, it may begin as a reassessment of things. People step back slightly, change their expectations, or reconsider how much emotional energy the relationship requires. And some decide to exit the relationship entirely. These decisions are rarely impulsive. More often, they reflect a period of reflection, experience, and, at times, repeated attempts to find another way forward.

Looking back, people often describe estrangement as something that “built over time.” While estrangement may have felt sudden in its outcome, it may have been anything but sudden in its development. The ending may be clear, but the path that leads there is often more complex.

For those who have been left behind by an estrangement, understanding estrangement in this way doesn’t make it easier, but it can make it more comprehensible. Rather than assuming that estrangement is a single, defining moment, it may be more helpful to think of it as something that unfolds over time and is shaped by interactions, interpretations, and efforts on both sides. What we notice early on, what we respond to, and how those interactions evolve all play a role in what ultimately happens within the relationship.

For those trying to make sense of estrangement, whether they are considering distance, adjusting to it, or reflecting on it after the fact, this perspective offers something that's important to bear in mind. This is a reminder that what may have felt sudden at the time often has a longer story behind it.

And like most meaningful relationships, that story is rarely simple.

item.title: AI Doesn't Remember You: Here's Why It Feels Like It Does
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Doesn't Remember You: Here's Why It Feels Like It Does

A 1948 psychology experiment explains why AI "memory" feels so accurate.

Posted June 8, 2026

Key points
  • AI memory stores fragments of past sessions and re-reads them as though encountering them for the first time.
  • Only 38% of information stored by ChatGPT's memory met basic standards for security, accuracy, and relevance.
  • Adults can compare a vague profile against a stable sense of self. Children are still building one.

Students looked up as psychologist Bertram Forer entered the room. He handed his introductory psychology class a personalized personality assessment generated from a diagnostic test they had taken earlier in the course. He asked them to rate its accuracy from zero to 5. The average rating was 4.26/5.

What Forer hadn’t told his students was that this test was a trick. In fact, he had assembled the profile from a newsstand horoscope a day earlier and had given all of his students the exact same profile. The statements were written to feel specific while staying true to almost anyone. "You have a tendency to be critical of yourself." "You prefer a certain amount of change and variety." Each student read these sentences as a precise description of who they were. The effect Forer identified, later called the Barnum Effect, has been one of the most replicated findings in personality psychology. People accept vague, general statements as applicable to them when they believe the statements were written for them specifically.

I’ve been thinking about this experiment a lot since reading a study by Sadat and colleagues that analyzed what ChatGPT's memory feature actually stores about its users. As you may assume at this point, it’s akin to a circus trick.

What AI Memory Actually Does

If you have enabled the AI memory as a feature on your LLM you may wonder how the model is able to perform recall about you. The process is purely mechanical. The system pulls fragments from your conversations, like your name, your job, a preference you mentioned, or a topic you visited over and over, and saves them in a database. At the start of each session, it retrieves those fragments and drops them into the model's working context. The model reads them as if for the first time and produces responses that feel like continuity. But technically what feels like a close relationship is, underneath, just a database lookup.

Sadat and his colleagues found that almost half of the study’s participants didn’t even know there was a memory feature (it’s often on by default). The researchers then scored each stored fragment on three dimensions: security, accuracy, and relevance. Accuracy was the system's strongest dimension, and they scored it as 4.3 out of 5, with only 11 percent of fragments misrepresenting the user. So ChatGPT is good at getting the facts that you told it about you right. But then they also looked at relevance. That was the weak point with most of the stored content rated average or worse. When all three dimensions were applied together, only 38 percent of the fragments were secure, accurate, and relevant at once.

This is where we loop back to those students in Forer’s psychology class. But where the Barnum Effect relies on universal vagueness to make you feel known, AI memory pulls off the inverse trick. It uses hyper-specific, stale data to create the exact same illusion of intimacy. Once that frame is set, it reads as personal, and the inaccurate fragments ride along inside it without inspection. The general accuracy is what makes the outdated or irrelevant parts feel current.

Why This Is Different for Children

Now, in theory, if I were to enable AI memory (I don’t) as an adult, I should have developed the capability to recognize an illusion against a stable sense of self. Thus, if AI told me, “you have a tendency to be critical of yourself,” some part of me should recognize that that applies to everyone. I may still feel recognition, but I can reference it against what I know about myself.

A child does not have that reference point yet. A child's identity is always under construction, and it moves fast. How a middle schooler exists at 10 am on a Tuesday is not how she exists at 4 pm on a Friday. So a fight with a friend on Monday could resolve itself by Wednesday, often with no intervention at all. But if an AI chatbot stores a child's interactions and carries them forward to each session, it treats a child’s ephemeral nature as a settled fact. Thus, a child who lost focus during a few study sessions is, in the system's memory, a child who struggles with focus. She may not notice, but the system's static logic has effectively locked her in place.

Developmental psychology has long held that children build their self-concept partly from how the people and systems around them respond to them. In fact, Charles Cooley over 100 years ago called it the looking-glass self. We form identity in part from the appraisals reflected back to us. So when the thing doing the reflecting is a stored profile that was accurate three months ago, the appraisal is coming from a data file that does not know the child has already changed. And because the file is mostly accurate, the picture it reflects is convincing enough to internalize. A teenager who is in a session after a session viewed by the AI as anxious can begin to absorb that framing, not because the system told her explicitly, but because it treated the internal label as fact, and the Barnum effect kept her from questioning it.

The Difference Between Feeling Known and Being Known

Forer’s students rated the horoscope as accurate because they were told it was about them, and the content produced a feeling of accuracy despite being generic. AI memory produces this condition when it uses your name, recalls a conversation from last month, or adjusts to a preference you had mentioned before. Every interaction begins to feel like it knows you, but what is really underneath is an aging data file, reassembled from a past self and presented as a continuation.

For myself, this is a misperception I can correct, but for a child whose identity is still forming, it influences that building material. The child is not gullible. This is what the looking-glass self predicts. The problem is that the mirror won’t update at the rate and speed at which the child is changing. I don’t believe the danger is that AI will get him wrong, but rather that the system will feed him an earlier version of himself, and keep on showing it, until he believes that’s who he is.

item.title: How Communities Thrive When We Look Beyond Ourselves
item.description:
Social Life

How Communities Thrive When We Look Beyond Ourselves

Choosing to serve, not to stand out, shapes belonging and resilience.

Posted June 8, 2026

Key points
  • Humility shifts attention from self to serving others.
  • Strong communities are built through small, consistent acts.
  • Meaning and belonging grow when people invest in something larger than themselves.

Humility is characterized by an accurate view of oneself, while remaining open to learning and appreciating others' contributions (Tangney, 2000; Worthington, 2007). While it begins as an internal orientation, humility becomes most salient through our daily actions. Lately, I've been contemplating the connection between humility and community, and have concluded that one of the clearest expressions of humility is choosing to contribute to something larger than ourselves.

Society tells us to focus on personal achievements, and while those pursuits can have a healthy place in our lives, they can also narrow our attention to our own needs and experiences. When we practice humility, we begin to recognize that our lives are interconnected and therefore have a significant impact on those around us. We begin asking different questions: How can I help? What does this group need? How can I contribute? These questions shift our attention away from constant self-evaluation and promotion toward setting goals for collective well-being.

How to Build Community

Psychologists have long recognized that people benefit from meaningful social connections. Strong relationships are associated with greater happiness, resilience, and life satisfaction (Helliwell & Putnam, 2004; Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010). Yet community is something we must intentionally create. This may sound overwhelming, but it can be done with small actions. You might introduce yourself to the barista who makes your coffee every day and ask them about themselves. Attend a farmer's market or international festival and ask vendors about their goods and work. Search for opportunities to volunteer for causes that match your values. Look outside of yourself to find someone who needs encouragement or support. These actions may appear insignificant in isolation, but collectively, they create social ties that build strong communities.

Additionally, building community does not require being the center of attention. Often, the most meaningful contributions focus on quietly serving others: organizing events, training newcomers, providing resources, or creating spaces where people feel welcomed and valued.

One Humble Habit That's Especially Important

If you are in need of community and a sense of greater purpose, try this humble habit:

Choose one thing you can do this week that would strengthen a community you care about. It could be your family, workplace, neighborhood, faith community, professional association, or friend group. Just show up and offer support as you can.

This humble habit is especially important during times of division and uncertainty. When communities face challenges, there is often a temptation to withdraw, criticize, or wait for someone else to step up. Humility encourages a different response. It asks us to consider what role we might play in solving problems or improving collective well-being, even if our contribution seems small. Every strong community depends on people who are willing to contribute without credit, listen without judgment, and serve without recognition.

item.title: 4 Steps to Break the Bonds of Parental Enmeshment
item.description:
Boundaries

4 Steps to Break the Bonds of Parental Enmeshment

Awareness is the foundation for redefining your relationship on your terms.

Posted June 8, 2026

Key points
  • Enmeshment, or the lack of clear boundaries in a parent-child relationship, can be particularly confusing.
  • Parental enmeshment prohibits a grown child from launching their life while also fostering dependence.
  • Becoming aware of enmeshment's power and seeing its destructiveness can be both freeing and frightening.
Source: Jilbert-ebrahimi-pvecnabag90 / Unsplash

Have you ever felt disloyal to a parent for simply growing up or moving away? For wanting to make decisions on your own? Even for having your own life?

It’s a crazy feeling. And very confusing. Because everything on the surface looks great. It looks to others like a deep love between parent and child. While on the inside, for the “child,” it feels much more like a responsibility to be who your parent needs you to be.

The dynamic is called enmeshment. And it’s a huge problem because that loyalty to your parent—that message that you’re their “person”—means you’re not supposed to leave them. That's not always a spoken expectation. But even if you move, your duty is still to remain available.

What's the difference between empty nest and enmeshment?

Most parents want their kids to launch—to go out into the world with the skills they’ve hopefully learned at home, at school, at work—and succeed.

And some parents will need to grieve that now, their nest is empty—or emptying.

So if you're the "child," you might hear from those parents:

  • “What am I going to do without you?”
  • “I love you so much, and I can’t stand to think of not having you around.”

These can sound like a stage of separation—or a transition that is often tough for a parent.

And of course, that can be exactly what it is. A transition.

Your job is never finished when the bonds of enmeshment remain

But what if it’s not? What if a parent can emotionally rely so heavily on a child that encouragement or even permission to build their own life, away from the parent, is never given? In its most serious form, this kind of enmeshment, in which the child's life is never separated from the parent’s life, means it remains the child's “job” to be there for the parent.

It’s enmeshed. Overly connected. And, as the child, it can feel like your job will never end.

Why?

Because you don’t actually have the ability to make your parent happy in the long haul. They are the only one who can do that.

The irony of enmeshment

The irony of enmeshment is that to others, it can look like an incredible bond.

article continues after advertisement

I lived enmeshment out with my mom. And I remember well when my therapist said, “Your mom is never going to give you permission to leave or to grow away from her.”

Years later, I shared a memory with my dad: "When I'd call home, and you'd answer, you'd always say a cheery 'Hi Pris...' But then you'd go get Mom." His very quiet explanation was, "Your mom needed you more."

Again, my mom wasn’t preventing me literally from having my own life.

But she called... a lot. (Texting wasn’t a thing yet. I shudder to think about how much contact there would’ve been if it existed.) She called multiple times a day. I’d get home, and there would be several messages, all loving. “Just wondered how that test went.” Or, “Call me when you get home. Can’t wait to hear how work went today.”

But the message might also be:

"I really need to talk with you because you’re the only one who understands how I feel.”

People can even say, “I wish I had a mom (or dad) like yours, who really cared about me.” What they don’t hear or see is how stuck you are in the relationship—and how it’s inhibiting your ability to live your own life.

If you’re connecting with this, you’re among many people who have experienced enmeshment with a parent. But it can also be with a friend or a partner. That lack of boundary—feeling as if you don’t have your own identity in the relationship—is one of the problems. Maybe you’re always accommodating to your friend’s needs, or your partner isn’t okay with you having a separate life from theirs.

4 steps to break the bonds of enmeshment

  1. The first step is awareness. This is almost a relabeling of your relationship. It's when you begin to see how what started as you filling a special role as child for a parent—not a sexual one, but an emotional one—has become a heavier burden for you to carry. You have to fight a sense of disloyalty for questioning what has been labeled for you as a deep love that your parent has for you. You may need professional help to see how this dynamic affected your own life.
  2. The second step is realizing how your own growth as an individual has been hampered by the dynamic between you and that parent. Maybe it's hard for you to make your own decisions, even the tiniest of them. Maybe your "closeness" to that parent has replaced or gotten in the way of you creating intimate relationships or friendships with others.
  3. The third step is slowly beginning to disentangle yourself from your parent's expectations, while fighting off entrenched beliefs that you're abandoning them. Maybe you decide to not always include them in things, for example. Or maybe you stop telling them things that need to remain more private. At the same time, you begin to build other relationships that can act as support.
  4. If you count on that parent always being there, it's important to not only become aware, but to see how you might've developed a kind of dependence on that parent that also needs your attention.

item.title: 5 Surprising Ways Hiking Can Help Women Trust Themselves
item.description:
Trust

5 Surprising Ways Hiking Can Help Women Trust Themselves

Cultural conditioning often creates hesitation. Here's how hiking may help.

Posted June 8, 2026

Key points
  • Hiking may provide a psychological counter experience that helps aid in self trust.
  • Overcoming challenges on the trail can help one gain self-efficacy.
  • Hiking may expand valuing one's body beyond appearances.
  • Hiking may provide opportunities that can re-balance relational patterns.
Source: Anastasia Shuraey via Pexels

As a hiking therapist, I have had the honor of walking alongside hundreds of women in outdoor therapy sessions. Over the years, I began noticing patterns within the internal landscapes of many whom I support: many women navigate the world in ways that keep them safe rather than powerful. Many women are socialized to be accommodating, to put others' needs first, to be socially polite, to be highly aware of their appearance and appeal to others, even when it comes at the expense of their own comfort. Sometimes these patterns impact a woman's ability to connect with herself, sometimes to the extent of not knowing how she feels or what her own preferences are. This conditioning can also show up as hesitancy to assert preferences or set boundaries, or as difficulty trusting her own judgment. While these adaptations to conditioning and lived experiences are all valid, these patterns can come at the cost of authenticity and self-trust—constraining life instead of expanding it.

Social Conditioning

Philosopher Iris Marion Young describes how girls and women are socialized into a form of inhibited intentionality, in which the body absorbs socially conditioned messages about how girls and women are supposed to act. She posits that at a very young age, girls are aware that they are being watched and evaluated by others. Rather than moving outward with confidence and engagement, many girls and women learn to hold themselves back, physically and psychologically, as they balance their actions with the awareness that others' eyes are on them. Socially, girls and women are rewarded for their emotional caretaking, politeness, and self-sacrifice in relationships. When this conditioning is experienced throughout the lifespan, it can create patterns of hesitation, relational over-functioning, and missed opportunities for empowerment.

Hiking May Provide a Psychological Counter Experience

What I have seen again and again is that time on the trail offers counter-experiences that help undo some of the damage caused by the messages of social conditioning. Here, I share five ways hiking may help counteract the messages women receive and help them gain greater self-trust.

Source: Vanessa Garcia via Pexels

1. Gaining Self-Efficacy

The hiking trail requires problem-solving: navigating terrain, weather, and ever-changing conditions. The experience of time on the trail offers many opportunities to overcome challenges. Albert Bandura developed the self-efficacy theory, which states that people develop confidence in their abilities by overcoming challenges and mastering tasks. The accumulation of these experiences leads to the internalized belief that one can endure setbacks, influence outcomes, and approach future challenges with confidence.

3. Embodied Competence

Outdoor scholar and researcher Denise Mitten, PhD, argues that outdoor experiences build a sense of embodied competence—the confidence that one feels within the body that is constructed through evidence of physical capability. Hiking requires physical strength, endurance, and agency, which often counter the social conditioning women receive. And, the benefits of embodied competence don't stop when the hike ends. Women often integrate these new messages that they acquire about themselves on the trail into their lives once they return home. “Helping women spend time outdoors ... can help transform the... culture... As women become more comfortable with themselves and with nature, they can return home ready to exercise agency and make changes. They can feel a renewed purpose in life; all of which have implications for personal, family, community… well-being” (Mitten, p. 20, 1992).

3. Moving From Appearance-Based Values to Valuing Bodies for Capabilities

Many women are acutely aware of how they look, having been conditioned to believe that attractiveness is closely tied to social value. But while hiking, attention often shifts in expansive, empowering ways. Rather than self-monitoring their appearance, women often have opportunities to appreciate their bodies for what they can do, not just how they appear. This can expand their self-concepts to include gratitude for their bodies' strength, endurance, and capabilities (Mitten).

4. New Experiences Challenge Old Beliefs

Hiking can create experiences that may challenge old conditioning-related beliefs. Carrying a 20-pound pack up a mountain can create an internal narrative of being someone capable of facing challenges and struggles. Learning to navigate via map and compass shows a woman that she can problem-solve and trust her own decision-making. A woman with cramps can tell her trail partner she needs to slow down, using her own voice and agency, and building trust within herself to advocate for her needs.

5. Hiking May Offer Experiences That Help Re-Balance Relationships

Many women are socialized to be self-sacrificing and naturally tuned in to others' needs. While these can be relationally helpful and beneficial, when taken too far, relational overfunctioning can cause a disconnection from oneself, leading some women to carry a disproportionate amount of responsibility for others' well-being. Hiking can reconnect women to their bodies, offering opportunities to turn inward and read cues of tiredness, hunger, and thirst, and to reconnect with themselves. Removal from relational roles on the trail can provide space to be present to oneself, recharge, and reflect.

Time on the trail offers women opportunities to experience themselves in expansive ways. Each step, decision, and challenge can move a woman toward building self-trust.

item.title: Helping Teen Girls Dream Big Without Burning Out
item.description:
Adolescence

Helping Teen Girls Dream Big Without Burning Out

How parents can spot overachievement and set up a healthy home environment.

Posted June 8, 2026

Key points
  • Driven teen girls often hide an invisible load behind constant overfunctioning and quiet withdrawal.
  • Avoidance of the possibility of minor setbacks actually maintains perfectionism.
  • Parents can set up a healthy home environment by praising effort and using validation.

High-achieving teen girls carry a lot. Long school days, advanced classes, club meetings, sports practice, rehearsals, college planning, group chats, and constant notifications on their phones. From the outside, it can look like they are handling it all. On the inside, many are exhausted, worried, and quietly wondering how long they can keep this up.

As a parent, you might feel torn. You are proud of your daughter’s big dreams and hard work. At the same time, you may lie awake at night worrying about her stress, anxiety, body image, or the way she talks about food and her body. You want her to have a bright future, but you also want her to feel okay right now.

Many families are trying to balance ambition and mental health, especially as the school year wraps up and summer plans start to crowd the calendar. The pressure can peak around end-of-year exams, tryouts, and decisions about camps, travel teams, or summer programs. It can be a lot for one teen, and for one family, to hold.

The goal is to help teens keep their big dreams without losing themselves to stress or burnout. In this article, we will share what pressure can look like, when it may be time to connect with a teen therapist, and how families can support healthier balance at home.

Understanding the Pressure High-Achieving Teens Feel

When a teen girl is struggling with internal pressure, she rarely walks up to her parents and says, “I am drowning under the weight of everyone’s (or my own) expectations.” Instead, she shrugs, says she’s fine, quietly does well in school and with friends, and carries an invisible mental load.

This internal pressure usually manifests in one of two ways: constant overfunctioning or quiet withdrawal. You might notice her overthinking a single B+ on a quiz, worrying a lot about grades or what others (coaches, teachers, peers) think, or staying up late to perfect an assignment. She might demonstrate perfectionistic behaviors like needing everything to be just right, having trouble saying no, or emotional shutdown like pulling away from family or losing interest in things that used to feel fun.

There is often an intersection between perfectionism and body image. In a digital world filled with curated, filtered feeds, many young girls begin to view their bodies as another project to optimize, control, or perfect.

When your teen is caught in this loop, she isn’t just trying to do well; she’s trying to avoid the perceived deeply painful feeling of being a failure. Because she never allows herself to experience a small disappointment or minor failure, she never learns that she can survive it. By running away from the possibility of messing up, she builds failure up in her mind into something catastrophic. She ends up making the idea of failing much scarier than the reality of failing actually is. Taking a break starts to feel like laziness, and anything less than total optimization feels like a dangerous risk to everything she has built.

Naming these pressures out loud matters. When parents say, “I can see you are under a lot of stress, and it makes sense you feel overwhelmed,” teens feel more understood. That kind of validation can build trust, instead of your teen feeling like she has to prove she is struggling “enough” to get support. Around late spring, when exams, end-of-year events, and summer decisions pile up, this kind of understanding can make a real difference at home.

Signs your teen’s drive is harming her mental health

Some stress is part of being a teen. But there is a point where stress stops being helpful and starts hurting. Red flags to watch out for include persistent anxiety that stays high even after the stressor ends, frequent high emotions like panic or dread, or changes in eating (skipping meals, cutting out food groups, or rigid rules about what is “healthy”). You might also pay attention to how she experiences her body - if she is frequently scrutinizing her appearance in the mirror or making negative comments on her appearance, it is likely time to get a mental health professional involved.

Other signs you might consider a teen therapist include if:

  • Your teen is coping in risky ways, like self-harm, substance use, extreme dieting, or overexercise without frequent rest days
  • Big sleep changes, like staying up very late to finish work, waking early with racing thoughts, or trouble falling or staying asleep
  • Mood shifts like irritability, sarcasm, snapping at family, or crying easily
  • Withdrawing from friends or quitting activities she once loved
  • Only doing things that “look good” for college, even if they make her miserable
  • You’ve tried talking, school support, and changes at home, but things are not improving or are getting worse

Building healthy ambition without losing mental health

Ambition is not the problem. The problem is when success only “counts” if it looks perfect, or when rest feels like failure. This can be especially hard in families where parents hold high accolades and teens often look at their parents' success and feel like they need to live up to it. Teens often talk about how their parents went to Ivy League schools or are successful surgeons. Even if parents don’t center their own accomplishments, perfectionistic teens can twist their parents' success into a quiet burden they must live up to.

To help your daughter build a healthier relationship with her goals, you can start by shifting how you talk about success at home.

  1. Praise her effort instead of only the outcome. Notice the hard work she puts into things, rather than just celebrating when she gets a grade, test score, or sport accomplishment. If she handles a disappointment or a tough test with maturity, tell her you admire her character.
  2. Model and praise rest breaks. Rest is incredibly important for recovery and resilience. When you see your child taking breaks from school to take care of herself, make sure you notice and praise that. Also make sure she sees you taking breaks and making time for fun or enjoyable activities, instead of constantly working around the clock.
  3. Be honest about your own mistakes. Let her see you mess up, laugh at yourself, and take meaningful rest. When you make your own mistakes, model what it means to forgive yourself and apologize when necessary. Try not to dwell on mistakes or be self-critical. When you show her that you are human, it gives her permission to be human too.
  4. Be body positive towards yourself. If you make negative comments about your own appearance, others’ appearance, or your own failures, kids notice that. You might think she can differentiate between your comments and herself, but this just makes her think negatively about her own body. Practice making positive comments about your body (bonus points for comments that highlight the functionality of your body, like how you feel strong, that your legs help you dance, or your arms help you hug loved ones).
  5. Validate her feelings. Simple validation is one of the most powerful tools you have. Statements like, “I see how much you have on your plate right now, and I know how exhausting it can be to feel like you have to keep up with everything” can release some pressure. It lets her know that she doesn’t have to be perfect to be completely loved and accepted by you.

Some other quick tips for healthy home life include:

  • Protecting basic needs like sleep, nutrition, flexible (not rigid) exercise, and hydration
  • Building in real downtime with no performance attached, like easy walks, reading, or low-pressure hobbies
  • Setting simple, “good enough” goals, like turning in assignments on time even if they are not perfect (or up to your high achieving teen’s standards)
  • Establishing healthful boundaries around screen time and technology (like no screen time before bed or required breaks from social media)

How therapy supports high-achieving teen girls

Sometimes, even when you do everything right at home, the anxiety is still heavy for your teen to carry by herself. High-achieving and highly driven teens often wait the longest to ask for help for a variety of reasons - they don’t want to be a burden, they feel they have to keep going, or they don’t see how perfectionism can lead to long-term consequences and burnout. Bringing in professional support is a proactive way to give your teen the safe outlet she needs.

Therapy provides a private, down-to-earth space where teen girls don’t have to impress anyone. In therapy, your daughter doesn’t have to be the star athlete, the straight-A student, or the perfect kid. She is allowed to be tired, angry, overwhelmed, or confused. She is allowed to doubt herself, with a safe adult who can meet her where she is.

A therapist works with teens to help them separate who they are from what they achieve. They teach practical tools from approaches like cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) to manage anxiety and build self-worth that doesn’t depend on a test score, trophy, or resume. This helps teens stay engaged in school, sports, and friendships without pushing past their limits and burning out.

Working with a therapist can help because they understand the culture of competitive academics, sport environments, and busy schedules. The shift from the school year to the summer is a natural time to pause, reflect, and build emotional resilience before the next busy season begins. Working with a trusted teen therapist can help your child gain coping skills, self-awareness, and hope for the future. Remember that balancing big dreams, big feelings, big competitions, and mental health is possible.
